[**Percentiles:**]{.blue} **Values** that divide data into **100 equal parts**. - [**Quartiles:**]{.blue} The 25th (**Q1**), 50th ([**Q2**]{.red} or [**median**]{.blue}), and 75th ([**Q3**]{.green}) percentiles. :::{.r-stack} :::{.vspace style="--space: -32px"} ![](img/percentiles.png) ::: :::{data-id="percentiles2" .fragment fragment-index=2 .vspace style="--space: -32px"} ![](img/percentiles2.png) ::: ::: :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} :::{.r-stack} :::{style="font-size: 80%" .fragment .fade-out fragment-index=2} ```{python} data[['Fare', 'Age']].describe().T.drop(columns=['count', 'mean', 'std']).round(2) ``` ::: :::{style="font-size: 80%" .fragment fragment-index=2} ```{python} data[['Fare', 'Age']].describe().T.drop(columns=['count', 'std']).round(2) ``` :::{.fragment fragment-index=3} - **Fare**: Mean >> Q2 suggesting [extremely large outliers]{.light-red} (some passengers paid very high fares). ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### Statistical values: Variance/Std {auto-animate="true"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 65%"} ```{python} #| echo: true data[['Age', 'Fare', 'SibSp', 'Parch']].head(3) ``` ::: :::{.vspace style="--space: -5px"} :::{style="font-size: 90%"} - There are [**two main Measures**]{.light-red} of [**Dispersion**]{.light-red} for describing how data points are spread out from the [**Mean**]{.blue}. ::: :::{.r-stack .vspace style="--space: -20px"} :::{.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1 style="font-size: 90%"} - [**Sample variance:**]{.blue} average of squared distances of data points from the [**Mean**]{.blue}. :::{.vspace style="--space: -40px"} [$$\color{blue}{\widehat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline{X})^2}.$$]{style="font-size: 80%"} ::: ::: :::{.fragment fragment-index=2 style="font-size: 90%"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -28px"} - [**Sample standard deviation (std):**]{.blue} Just the square root of [**Variance**]{.blue}. :::{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} [$$\color{blue}{\widehat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline{X})^2}}.$$]{style="font-size: 75%"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} #### Examples: ```{python} #| echo: false import numpy as np import plotly.express as px # Assuming 'data' is already defined earlier in your script df1 = pd.DataFrame({ 'x' : list(data['Age']+data['Age'].mean()*0.7) + [data['Age'].mean()*1.7, data['Age'].median()*1.7] +\ list(data['Age'].values*1.72) + [data['Age'].mean()*1.7, data['Age'].median()*1.7], 'y': list(np.random.normal(1, 0.01, size=data.shape[0]+2)) +\ list(np.random.normal(2, 0.01, size=data.shape[0]+2)), 'Variable': list(['Variable 1']*data.shape[0]) + ['Mean 1', 'Median 1'] + list(['Variable 2']*data.shape[0]) + ['Mean 2', 'Median 2'] }) # 1. Calculate Variance and Std Dev (filtering out the Mean/Median points) var1 = df1[df1['Variable'] == 'Variable 1']['x'].var() std1 = df1[df1['Variable'] == 'Variable 1']['x'].std() var2 = df1[df1['Variable'] == 'Variable 2']['x'].var() std2 = df1[df1['Variable'] == 'Variable 2']['x'].std() # 2. Find the max X value to align the text neatly on the right side text_x_pos = df1['x'].max() # 3. Create the figure fig = px.scatter( df1, x='x', y='y', color='Variable', symbol='Variable', symbol_map={'Variable 1': 'circle', 'Mean 1': 'x', 'Median 1': 'diamond', 'Variable 2': 'circle', 'Mean 2': 'x', 'Median 2': 'diamond'}, title="Dot plot of Variable 1 and Variable 2" ) # 4. Add Annotations for Variable 1 (y-level is roughly 1) fig.add_annotation( x=text_x_pos, y=1, text=f"Var: {var1:.2f}
Std: {std1:.2f}", showarrow=False, xanchor="left", yshift=20, # Shift slightly up so it doesn't overlap the dots font=dict(size=10, color="#1f77b4") # Match plotly's default blue ) # 5. Add Annotations for Variable 2 (y-level is roughly 2) fig.add_annotation( x=text_x_pos, y=2, text=f"Var: {var2:.2f}
Std: {std2:.2f}", showarrow=False, xanchor="left", yshift=20, font=dict(size=10, color="#d62728") # Match plotly's default red ) # 6. Update layout (increased width and right margin to fit the text) fig.update_layout( height=220, width=400, # Widened slightly from 400 to fit annotations margin=dict(r=80) # Add padding to the right ) fig.show() ``` :::{.r-stack} :::{.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1} :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px" style="font-size: 63%"} ```{python} #| echo: true var = data[['Age','Fare']].var().to_frame().round(5) var.columns = ['Var'] var.T ``` ::: :::{style="font-size: 90%"} - Large variance means that [**data points are widely spread out from the Mean**]{.blue}. ::: ::: :::{.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2} :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px" style="font-size: 63%"} ```{python} #| echo: true std = data[['Age','Fare']].apply(['var', 'std']) std ``` ::: :::{style="font-size: 90%"} - [**Std**]{.blue} is more interpretable than variance because it has the same unit as $X_i$. ::: ::: :::{.fragment .fade-in fragment-index=3} :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} ![Intuition of Variance and Standard Deviation.](img/var.mp4){#video-var fig-align="center"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### Statistical Summary :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 70%"} ```{python} data[['Age', 'Fare', 'SibSp', 'Parch']].head(3) ``` ::: :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} > [**Statistical summary**]{.blue} uses all key values to help us understand how the data is distributed and detect any potential problems with it. - Where the data is concentrated (**mean/median**)? - How spread out it is (**var/std**)? - Any extreme values (**mean vs median**)? - Any invalid values (**min/max**)? ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%" .fragment} #### Examples: ![](img/percentiles3.png){.up1} :::{style="font-size: 68%"} ```{python} #| echo: true data[['Age','Fare']]\ .describe().drop('count') # for summary ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### [Visualization: Boxplot]{.light-blue} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} ```{python} data[['Age', 'Fare', 'SibSp', 'Parch']].head(7) ``` ::: ![](img/boxplot.svg){fig-align="center"} ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -20px" .incremental} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - Boxplots describe the data distribution using [**Quartiles**]{.blue} and the [**range**]{.blue} where data normally fall within: - [**Lower**]{.blue} and [**upper part of the box**]{.blue} are $Q_1$ and $\color{green}{Q_3}$. - [**Median**]{.blue} $\color{red}{Q_2}$ is the middle line. - [**Interquartile range:**]{.blue} $\text{IQR}=\color{green}{Q_3}-Q_1$ (gap of $50\%$ most important part of the data). - [**Range:**]{.blue} [$[Q_1-1.5\text{IQR},\color{green}{Q_3}+1.5\text{IQR}]$]{style="font-size: 80%"}. If the data are [**normally distributed**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution){target="_blank"}, $99.3\%$ of data fall within this range. - [**Outliers:**]{.blue} data points that [**fall outside**]{.light-red} of the range. ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### [Visualization: Boxplot (Example)]{.light-blue} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} ```{python} data[['Age', 'Fare', 'SibSp', 'Parch']].head(6) ``` ::: :::{style="font-size: 80%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: "center" import plotly.express as px fig = px.box(data, x="Fare") fig.update_layout(height=200, width=450, title="Boxplot of Fare") fig.show() ``` ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.r-stack} :::{.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1} - Boxplots describe the data distribution using [**Quartiles**]{.blue} and the [**range**]{.blue} where data normally fall within: - [**Lower**]{.blue} and [**upper part of the box**]{.blue} are $Q_1$ and $\color{green}{Q_3}$. - [**Median**]{.blue} $\color{red}{Q_2}$ is the middle line. - [**Interquartile range:**]{.blue} $\text{IQR}=\color{green}{Q_3}-Q_1$ (gap of $50\%$ most important part of the data). - [**Range:**]{.blue} [$[Q_1-1.5\text{IQR},\color{green}{Q_3}+1.5\text{IQR}]$]{style="font-size: 80%"}. If the data are [**normally distributed**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution){target="_blank"}, $99.3\%$ of data fall within this range. - [**Outliers:**]{.blue} data points that [**fall outside**]{.light-red} of the range. ::: :::{.fragment fragment-index=1 .incremental} - Fares range from $£0$ to maximum fare of $£512.33$. - $Q_1=£7.9$ indicating that around $25\%$ of passengers spent less than $£7.9$ to get to the ship. - $\color{red}{Q_2}=£14.45$ (**Median**): around $50\%$ spent less than $£14.45$. - $\color{green}{Q_3}=£31$: around $75\%$ spent less than $£31$. - [**Outliers**]{.blue}: Passengers who spent more than the upper fence ($£65$), with the largest fare of $£512.33$. ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### Visualization: Histogram :::{style="font-size: 70%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: "center" import plotly.express as px # Calculate the mean and median mean_age = data["Age"].mean() median_age = data["Age"].median() # Create the base histogram fig = px.histogram(data, x="Age") # Add a vertical dashed line for the Mean fig.add_vline( x=mean_age, line_dash="dash", line_color="red", annotation_text=f"Mean: {mean_age:.1f}", annotation_position="top right" ) # Add a vertical dashed line for the Median fig.add_vline( x=median_age, line_dash="dash", line_color="green", annotation_text=f"Median: {median_age:.1f}", annotation_position="top left" ) # Apply your layout settings fig.update_layout( height=220, width=500, title="Histogram of Age" ) fig.show() ``` - A histogram is constructed by: - Defining a grid range of bins: $B_1, \dots, B_N$. - The height of each bar represents the **count/frequency** of $X_i$ values that fall within the corresponding bin. ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{style="font-size: 90%" .fragment} [**Mathematical definition of histogram**]{.blue} - Define bins: $B_1,\dots, B_N$. - For any $x$ such that $x\in B_k$ for some $k$, $$\text{hist}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{1}_{\{X_i\in B_k\}}.$$ where $\mathbb{1}_{\{X_i\in B_k\}}$ is an indicator function that equals $1$ if $X_i$ falls within the bin $B_k$, and $0$ otherwise. ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### Visualization: Kernel Density Plot (KDE) :::{style="font-size: 70%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{data-id="boxplot1" style="font-size: 90%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: "center" import plotly.figure_factory as ff age = [data[['Age']].dropna().values.reshape(-1)] group_labels = ['distplot'] fig = ff.create_distplot(age, group_labels=group_labels, bin_size=1.9) fig.update_layout(height=220, width=500, title="Histogram of Age") fig.show() ``` ::: - A **Kernel Density Plot** is a smooth, continuous version of a **histogram**. - It describes the relative frequency of observations over ranges of values. - It has nicer mathematical properties than histograms. ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{style="font-size: 90%" .fragment} [**Mathematical definition of KDE**]{.blue} - If $K$ is a smooth kernel function, for example: $K(x)=e^{-x^2/2}$. - For a given $h>0$ and for any $x$: $$\text{kde}(x)=\frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^nK\Big(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\Big).$$ ------ - **Kernel density plot** conveys similar information as **histograms**. - It highlights common ranges of values and patterns in the data. ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### Summary :::{.columns} :::{.column width="70%"} ![](img/quan.png){fig-align="center"} ::: :::{.column width="30%"} :::{style="font-size: 70%" .incremental} - [**Univariate analysis**]{.blue} aims at **describing**, **understanding** and **detecting** potential [problems]{.red} in the data by looking at each variable separately. - [**Descriptive statistics**]{.blue} and [**visualization**]{.blue} are the two main tools for univariate analysis. ::: ::: ::: --- ### [Qualitative]{.red} columns of [Titanic Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/yasserh/titanic-dataset){target="_blank"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="40%" style="font-size: 80%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true qual_var = ['Survived', 'Pclass', 'Sex'] import plotly.express as px import plotly.graph_objects as go from plotly.subplots import make_subplots fig = make_subplots( rows=3, cols=1, specs=[[{"type": "bar"}], [{"type": "bar"}], [{"type": "bar"}]], subplot_titles=("Barplot of Survived", "Barplot of Pclass ", "Barplot Sex")) for i, va in enumerate(qual_var): cnt = data[va].value_counts() if i == 0: fig.add_trace( go.Bar(x=list(cnt.index.astype(str)), y=list(cnt.values), name=va), col=1, row=i+1) else: fig.add_trace( go.Bar(x=list(cnt.index.astype(object)), y=list(cnt.values), name=va), col=1, row=i+1) fig.update_layout(height=450, width=450) fig.show() ``` ::: :::{.column width="60%" style="font-size: 80%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true fig = make_subplots( rows=3, cols=1, specs=[[{"type": "pie"}], [{"type": "pie"}], [{"type": "pie"}]], subplot_titles=("Pie chart of Survived", "Pie chart of Pclass ", "Pie chart Sex")) for i, va in enumerate(qual_var): cnt = data[va].value_counts() fig.add_trace(go.Pie(labels=list(cnt.index.astype(object)), values=list(cnt.values)), col=1, row=i+1) fig.update_layout(height=450, width=450) fig.show() ``` ::: ::: --- ### [Quantitative]{.blue} columns :::{style="font-size: 80%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true quan_var = ['Age', 'SibSp', 'Parch', 'Fare'] cols = ['#C96451', '#80C96F', '#6B7FDB', '#C07EDE'] fig = make_subplots( rows=2, cols=4, subplot_titles=("Distribution of Age", "Distribution of Parch", "Distribution of SibSp", "Distribution of Fare", "","","","")) for i, va in enumerate(quan_var): fig.add_trace( go.Box(x=data[va].values, name=va, marker_color = cols[i]), col=i+1, row=1) fig.add_trace( go.Histogram(x=data[va].values, name=va, marker_color = cols[i]), col=i+1, row=2) fig.update_layout(height=450, width=1000) fig.show() ``` ::: --- ### Quantitative columns (log scale) :::{style="font-size: 80%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true quan_var = ['Age', SibSp", "Distribution of log(Fare)", "","","","")) for i, va in enumerate(quan_var): fig.add_trace( go.Box(x=data[va].values, name=va, marker_color = cols[i]), col=i+1, row=1) fig.add_trace( go.Histogram(x=data[va].values, name=va, marker_color = cols[i]), col=i+1, row=2) fig.update_layout(height=450, width=1000) fig.update_xaxes(type="log", row=1, col=4) fig.update_yaxes(type="log",
